articles.title: The final regular-season Pecking Order: Mossdeep finishes first
articles.dek: Thirty-two clubs, seventeen results apiece, and a clear leading pair before the postseason begins.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Mossdeep and Saffron finish first and second. This is my final ranking of regular-season strength, considering the full schedule, recent performance and the personnel involved. It is separate from the seeded bracket and from the championship-route ranking below. Planned rest matters when interpreting Mossdeep’s last two games; a win remains a win when the younger players deliver it.

rankings.themeLabel: Seventeen wins, with useful work behind the starters.
rankings.text: Michael Dorrill’s confirmed rest-and-development finish produced a 22–3 win and a 27–0 shutout. Budew Baker threw three touchdowns in the finale; Shawn Mareman rushed for 153 yards. Dram Marino’s fifty-six-touchdown season and the league’s best scoring defense keep the Eclipse first. Poury Holt’s absence remains a real cost.

rankings.themeLabel: The strongest challenger finishes emphatically.
rankings.text: Archam Manning threw five touchdowns, HeeDee Lamb caught three and NeMarcus Tare recorded six sacks in a 49–10 win. The Psi Corps finish with 597 points scored and 138 allowed. Their second seed requires an extra playoff game, but this ranking rewards their whole-season strength and healthy current roster.

rankings.themeLabel: A bye earned before an uncomfortable finale.
rankings.text: Mt. Silver’s 21–13 loss to Cianwood does not erase fourteen wins or the head-to-head victory over Saffron. It does expose the strain of the injury list: Crem Ftzpatrik threw for 160 yards without a touchdown. Garshawn Lynch remains productive. The Reds need the week off to yield a coherent available offense.

rankings.themeLabel: Thirteen wins, then a receiving problem.
rankings.text: The Starseekers rushed for 213 yards and held Veilstone to ninety-five total in a 23–3 win. That is a strong final defensive statement. The sixteen-week absence for 88 Special removes ten season receiving touchdowns, placing greater responsibility on Fera LaGatr and the available receivers before Hearthome arrives.

rankings.themeLabel: Four straight wins carry a fourth seed.
rankings.text: The Blaze beat Pewter 13–7 after more expansive wins over Mt. Silver and Blackthorn. Gholdengo’s thirty passing touchdowns support the case that Cinnabar can threaten better-seeded teams. Exploud’s six-week absence makes the immediate Blackthorn rematch more difficult than the earlier result alone suggests.

rankings.themeLabel: Eight straight, and a division won at the last kick.
rankings.text: Lavender’s 21–20 victory required a fourth-down conversion, a late touchdown and a fifty-one-yard field goal. The eight-game streak is persuasive; the season’s plus-eight point differential also warns how often the Wails have needed a precise finish. They earned the home playoff game against Vermilion.

rankings.themeLabel: One point changed the route.
rankings.text: Hatterene threw for 301 yards, but Lavender’s last drive turned a division title into a fifth seed. The Dragons still have twelve wins and a productive passing attack. Their 348 points allowed leave less protection for a close-game offense than the higher clubs on this list enjoy.

rankings.themeLabel: Thirty-five points earn the better wild-card trip.
rankings.text: Dewford beat Rustboro 35–29, converting eight of eleven third downs and receiving a kickoff-return touchdown from Meowscarada. The fifth seed sends the Breakers to Eterna. A healthy current roster and several ways to score lift them above the lower-scoring division champions immediately below.

rankings.themeLabel: Twelve wins, with little spare margin.
rankings.text: The Pride beat Mauville 13–7 and will host Rustboro for the third meeting of the season. Petalburg won the first two. Its 286 points scored and 292 allowed make the record unusual, while Oinkologne’s continued absence complicates the effort to produce another controlled, low-scoring win.

rankings.themeLabel: The defense has made eleven wins possible.
rankings.text: A 9–3 victory completed a season with 184 points allowed. Tatsugiri, Stantler and now Dewgong have positive-week absences. The Thorns get a home playoff game, but the available offense must offer more support against Dewford’s multiple scoring threats than a single-digit finale required.

rankings.themeLabel: The offense travels; the defensive questions travel too.
rankings.text: Shawn Watzon threw for 296 yards without an interception and Gibby Timmy caught 148, yet Rustboro lost 35–29. The Stone finish 9–8. Their explosive receiving plays give them a plausible upset route, while the third-down and return concessions in the finale explain why it remains an upset pick.

rankings.themeLabel: Ten wins earned through tight finishes.
rankings.text: A 13–10 victory at Cerulean secured sixth seed. The Volts’ 210 points scored and 287 allowed are a warning about their scoring ceiling, particularly with Drakloak still out. Repeated close wins deserve credit; they do not make the trip to an eight-win-streak Lavender offense comfortable.

rankings.themeLabel: The required win arrived as a shutout.
rankings.text: Olivine beat Azalea 17–0 and qualified without help. Gabite’s new eight-week absence joins continuing backfield losses before the trip to Saffron. Nine wins earn a place in the tournament; the 220-point season and current availability keep the Ironclads near its lower edge in strength.

rankings.themeLabel: The final berth belongs to the team that finished its part.
rankings.text: Hearthome beat Pastoria 21–13 while Mauville and Canalave lost. The 8–8–1 record becomes a seventh seed and a visit to Sunyshore. The Haunts have won their final two games, but must produce a stronger answer to a thirteen-win opponent than their season-long minus-twenty-five margin suggests.

rankings.themeLabel: An upset worth recognizing after elimination.
rankings.text: Crobat scored on a ninety-eight-yard kickoff return and caught two touchdowns in a 21–13 win at Mt. Silver. Cianwood finished 8–9 and outside the field. The final result moves the Crushers above other eliminated clubs here without pretending it changed the qualifying table.

rankings.themeLabel: A six-point loss ended the controllable route.
rankings.text: The Dynamos could qualify by winning at Petalburg and lost 13–7. Their 248 points scored and 262 allowed describe a competitive 8–9 team whose final offensive possession count never became enough points. Hearthome’s victory completed the consequence.

rankings.themeLabel: Two damaging losses closed the schedule.
rankings.text: Mahogany won 27–13 after Lavender’s 51–10 victory the previous week. Violet finished 8–9, with 314 points allowed. The Falcons remained relevant late into the race, but the last two performances leave a substantial gap between that opportunity and the final ranking.

rankings.themeLabel: The final road win improves the ending.
rankings.text: Celadon beat Viridian 21–10 and finished 6–11 with a minus-thirty-seven differential. The defense allowed 244 points, better than several clubs with more wins. The 207-point offense kept that defensive work from becoming a postseason place.

rankings.themeLabel: The defense kept another game within reach.
rankings.text: Cinnabar won 13–7, leaving Pewter 6–11. The Rockers allowed 243 points and scored 181. Their final two results, a win at Viridian and this close loss, illustrate a competitive defense with too little consistent scoring behind it.

rankings.themeLabel: A one-point win closes a difficult division season.
rankings.text: The Surge beat Fortree 17–16 and finished 7–10. Drampa’s 3,169 passing yards and twenty-five touchdowns give the offense a meaningful individual season. The team’s 354 points allowed kept that production from supporting a winning record.

rankings.themeLabel: Mossdeep ended the late recovery decisively.
rankings.text: The Inferno’s three-game winning streak ended in a 27–0 loss. Lavaridge managed 132 yards and nineteen rushing yards against an opponent using its confirmed development plan. Seven wins remain, but the finale reinforces the distance to the division leader.

rankings.themeLabel: The necessary victory never arrived.
rankings.text: Oreburgh won 14–10 and Canalave finished 8–9. Injuries had complicated the last assignment, and the season’s 183 points scored left little room for another missed chance. The Bulwark’s record stays respectable while the final scoring profile limits this ranking.

rankings.themeLabel: A useful final win against a team with stakes.
rankings.text: The Frost beat Violet 27–13 and finished 5–11–1. Their defensive playmakers, including Lopunny, supplied individual seasons worth honoring. The ending lifts Mahogany here without making the larger losing record disappear.

rankings.themeLabel: The narrow last route ended at home.
rankings.text: Vermilion won 13–10, leaving the Tide 7–10. The playoff condition required a win and help; Cerulean did not complete its own part. Its 365 points allowed provide a season-long explanation for why seven wins required so much offensive recovery.

rankings.themeLabel: The final offense could not sustain a challenge.
rankings.text: Sunyshore held the Fists to ninety-five yards in a 23–3 loss. Ponyta and Vigoroth supplied productive rookie seasons, but the club finished 6–11 with 185 points scored. Those individual cases belong on awards ballots without turning into a claim of team strength.

rankings.themeLabel: Hearthome found the scores it needed.
rankings.text: The Waves lost 21–13 and finished 6–11. Kilowattrel’s thirty-one special-teams tackles offer a separate individual achievement. The final result also closes the week in which Pastoria could still affect a rival’s invitation.

rankings.themeLabel: The backfield workload did not produce enough points.
rankings.text: Celadon won 21–10 in the finale. Gabite’s 1,126 rushing yards and Sigilyph’s eleven interceptions are substantial individual totals on a 5–12 club. The Titans could generate useful work in isolated areas without combining it into consistent wins.

rankings.themeLabel: A close loss leaves four wins.
rankings.text: Sootopolis won 17–16. Fortree had conceded only seven points the previous week and still lost, so the two finales contain different immediate problems. Across the season, the Skyhawks could not make enough scoring and defensive work coincide.

rankings.themeLabel: Three points finished the schedule.
rankings.text: Eterna won 9–3. Snowpoint’s Drampa threw twenty touchdowns against seven interceptions over the season, and Oinkologne rushed for 943 yards. Those useful totals never became enough team scoring to escape a four-win finish.

rankings.themeLabel: The final win changed another club’s season.
rankings.text: The Miners beat Canalave 14–10 and helped decide the last Hoenn–Sinnoh berth. Drednaw’s 11.5 sacks stand out as an individual achievement. Four wins still place Oreburgh low, but the final afternoon gave its supporters a consequential result.

rankings.themeLabel: The final shutout confirmed the scoring problem.
rankings.text: Olivine won 17–0 after Mt. Silver’s 41–9 victory the prior week. Azalea could not make a playoff-seeking visitor earn a high score. The ending leaves little basis for lifting the Swarm in the final regular-season order.

rankings.themeLabel: Saffron ended the season with seven touchdowns.
rankings.text: The Shadows lost 49–10 and finished 3–14. Heatmor’s 850 receiving yards remain worthy of individual consideration. Six sacks conceded to Tare in the finale supply a direct example of the protection problems that made the scoring task harder.

articles.title: The fourteen championship routes, ranked
articles.dek: A separate postseason judgment: byes, opponents and confirmed availability change the path from a good season to the Indigo Bowl.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: This ranking judges the remaining championship routes, not the completed league table. It is an editorial order rather than simulated odds. The two top seeds need three wins; every other entrant needs four. Reseeding sends each first seed the lowest surviving conference seed, so the next opponent remains conditional.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: A bye and home field put the 17–0 team three wins from a championship. Marino’s efficient season and the defense’s 130 points allowed make this the strongest route. The planned late rest supplied experience to Baker and Mareman; Holt’s absence still removes one option.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: The Psi Corps have to win four games, but begin against an injured Olivine team. Their healthy current roster and 459-point differential outweigh the extra round in my ordering. The likely obstacles are Lavender, the Kanto–Johto survivor and then Mossdeep.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: The first seed is valuable: one fewer game, and the lowest surviving Kanto–Johto seed comes to Mt. Silver. The extensive injury list is why the Reds remain behind Saffron in this judgment. Their 36–33 win over the Psi Corps establishes a viable route if the available offense can function.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: Hearthome comes first, then a potential second home game. The 88 Special absence weakens a thirteen-win team before the difficult part of the route. Sunyshore’s rushing and defensive finale support confidence in the opening assignment; a possible trip to Mossdeep remains the largest obstacle.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: The Blaze have already beaten Blackthorn and Mt. Silver, two plausible first opponents. Exploud’s absence makes the rematch harder, and Saffron’s 35–3 regular-season win warns against projecting the same offense through every matchup. Four straight victories still give this route credibility.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: Eight consecutive wins and a home opener place Lavender above most wild cards. If Saffron also wins, the Wails must visit the Psi Corps next. Moth Ball’s growing contribution is encouraging; the narrow season scoring margin and Mr. Clanky’s continued absence keep the route demanding.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: A healthy current roster draws an Eterna team missing several productive players. The Breakers can score through rushing, passing and returns. An opening win is plausible, but reseeding may send them straight to Mossdeep; the exact opponent depends on the other results.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: Hatterene gives the Dragons a credible passing chance at Cinnabar. Losing the division means every likely Kanto–Johto assignment is away from home. The one-point finale defeat does not destroy the team, but its defensive concessions make a four-win championship sequence difficult.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: A home game against a team it has already beaten twice is useful. Oinkologne’s absence and the season’s negative point differential temper the twelve-win record. If the Pride advance, a higher seed is likely to require more offensive production than their recent narrow victories.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: The defense and home field make the Thorns a live opening-round opponent. Tatsugiri, Stantler and Dewgong are currently out, leaving less room for the offense to answer a quick Dewford score. Eterna must first make its preferred low-scoring game happen.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: The sixth seed can win a passing exchange at Petalburg, but the Stone have lost both prior meetings. Watzon and Timmy provide a concrete route to an upset. Allowing thirty-five to Dewford makes the defensive requirement equally concrete, before any possible Mossdeep trip.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: The Volts have ten wins and an ability to survive close finishes. They need that pattern at Lavender, where the home team has won eight straight. Drakloak’s absence reduces an offense that already scored only 210 points; the opening upset requires limiting possessions and finishing its own.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: The Ironclads qualified with a shutout, then drew Saffron while losing Gabite. They need a major reversal of the offensive comparison simply to reach the next round. The defense must keep the opener manageable while the available backfield finds a way to sustain drives.

rankings.themeLabel: Championship route
rankings.text: The Haunts earned the last invitation by winning while two rivals lost. Sunyshore’s 88 Special absence gives them a changed opponent, but the thirteen-win home team still has a strong defensive and rushing case. A seventh seed faces four wins without expected home-field help.

articles.title: The Rook Board: six tight ends, three different workout leaders
articles.dek: Dhelmise leads the disclosed range and bench; Arctozolt runs the quickest forty; Trubbish changes direction fastest.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: The available tight-end board contains six prospects, all covered here. Dhelmise’s 80–99 disclosed range gives Santalune the first evaluation, but the athletic comparisons are sufficiently different to make a single generic tight-end workout unhelpful. A club should define the intended receiving and blocking responsibilities before deciding which measurements deserve the most weight.

The order begins with the visible scouting ranges. The accompanying judgments use only the disclosed combine, age and school assignments. These are evaluation priorities, not a prediction of the draft order or a claim about hidden ability. No college statistics or game film have been invented to complete the profiles.

Tight ends remain relevant while the professional playoffs begin. Gyarzalez’s injury changes Mt. Silver’s available passing game, Exploud’s absence changes Cinnabar’s, and Gronkaludon’s receiving production remains part of Mossdeep’s championship case. Those examples show the range of responsibility a club may be trying to fill. They do not mean every prospect below can supply the same job.

prospects.name: Dhelmise
prospects.analysis: Santalune’s Dhelmise leads the available tight-end ranges at 80–99 and the group’s bench results with twenty-eight repetitions. The immediate evaluation should establish how that strength translates to an attached blocking assignment and whether the receiver can become available on schedule. The 5.06 forty and 7.24 cone point toward testing a defined job before promising every route.
prospects.concern: The thirty-inch vertical and slower cone leave receiving movement questions unresolved. Strength measurements do not certify blocking technique.
prospects.projection: First tight-end evaluation; test blocking and receiving responsibilities separately.

prospects.name: Arctozolt
prospects.analysis: Lavender Forest’s Arctozolt has a 67–95 range and the quickest forty among these six at 4.87. Twenty bench repetitions offer another useful comparison with Dhelmise. Put both prospects through the same release, contact and route assignments to learn whether Arctozolt’s straight-line advantage survives a more complicated job.
prospects.concern: The 7.18 cone and thirty-one-inch vertical do not establish a broad movement advantage.
prospects.projection: Early comparison with Dhelmise for clubs needing a more mobile option.

prospects.name: Trubbish
prospects.analysis: Cascarrafa’s Trubbish combines a 56–84 range with the quickest cone in this group, 6.77, and a thirty-six-inch vertical. The 4.91 forty also places near the front. That movement profile warrants receiving work against the higher-range pair rather than dismissal based on the order alone.
prospects.concern: Fifteen bench repetitions trail the two leaders. Contact technique and receiving consistency remain unverified.
prospects.projection: Priority receiving-role workout within the tight-end pool.

prospects.name: Clamperl
prospects.analysis: Hulbury’s Clamperl brings sixteen bench repetitions and a 45–73 range. A club considering a narrow attached role should test whether the prospect can execute it repeatedly, then compare the result with the faster candidates. The published measurements make a broad movement projection difficult.
prospects.concern: A 5.20 forty, 7.31 cone and twenty-eight-inch vertical are the slowest or lowest marks in this six-player group.
prospects.projection: Defined-role evaluation before a broader roster commitment.

prospects.name: Sizzlipede
prospects.analysis: Stow-on-Side’s Sizzlipede has a 34–62 range, five-second forty and 6.96 cone. Those movement marks are more competitive than the six bench repetitions. The workout should separate route availability from contact demands so one promising drill does not become an unsupported complete-player conclusion.
prospects.concern: The strength measurement leaves substantial contact-work uncertainty.
prospects.projection: Receiving-oriented comparison with the lower-range candidates.

prospects.name: Oshawott
prospects.analysis: Gateon State’s Oshawott has a 28–56 range but the highest vertical here, thirty-seven inches. Nine bench repetitions and a 6.95 cone give specific comparison points with Sizzlipede. The jump result earns a catch-point examination; it does not erase the lower disclosed range.
prospects.concern: No recorded receiving production or blocking grade establishes how the workout translates to a professional assignment.

art.alt: The tight-end evaluation combines receiving and blocking questions. Conceptual college practice-field illustration.

articles.title: Fourteen teams, five brackets, one Indigo Bowl
articles.dek: The PSPN staff commits: three picks for Mossdeep, one for Saffron and one for Mt. Silver, with every round and every upset explained.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Fourteen clubs remain. Five writers have committed to every winner through the Indigo Bowl, using the confirmed seeds and reseeding after the wild-card round. The tables are original postseason forecasts, frozen here before the first game; later round previews will be new judgments rather than edits to these brackets.
Mara Voss — Mossdeep has earned the burden

I am picking Mossdeep because Michael Dorrill has built an offense that can change personnel and still give the defense a useful game. The Eclipse finished 17–0, scored 724 points and allowed 130. Dram Marino threw fifty-six touchdown passes against four interceptions in fifteen appearances. That is an enormous advantage before anybody starts asking how frightened an undefeated team ought to be of its own record. I want the opponents to explain how they intend to stop it.

The last two weeks matter because Dorrill deliberately rested starters and gave younger players work. Budew Baker threw two touchdowns against Sootopolis and three at Lavaridge. Those wins do not prove the postseason lineup should be built around him. They show that the staff could pursue development without surrendering its control of the games. A championship run should benefit from that work when a reserve has to enter, even though no coach gets to choose the moment an injury arrives.

My first difficult call comes in Cinnabar. I take Blackthorn by three because Hatterene’s 377 completions and eight interceptions give the Dragons a credible route through an uncomfortable road game. Cinnabar beat them earlier, and I accept that evidence. I also have to account for the new loss of Exploud and his 657 receiving yards. The rematch is being played by the available teams. It is the biggest wild-card upset on my bracket, and the one most likely to make me cross something out immediately.

Reseeding sends Blackthorn to Mt. Silver if my other picks hold. I give the Reds that game, then take Saffron in the conference championship. Archam Manning’s offense can score on Mt. Silver; the 36–33 regular-season loss established that much. The Reds’ injured quarterback and tight-end group makes repeating thirty-six a larger demand. Saffron has no positive-week injury entries in this export, and the healthy group has been producing on both sides of the ball.

Saffron is the opponent most likely to stop my champion. Mossdeep beat it 20–17 in Week 10, a result that supplies a warning as well as reassurance. NeMarcus Tare and Chen Norton Jr finished with fifty-two combined sacks. If the Eclipse lose control of protection and keep asking Marino to solve long downs, this becomes a much less comfortable argument. Accel BeckhmJr’s 1,953 receiving yards do not excuse a missed assignment before the ball leaves the quarterback.

I take Mossdeep over Dewford and Sunyshore, then 34–27 over Saffron. Dewford already pushed the Eclipse to 24–21, and Sunyshore has the conference’s second seed for a reason. I am not forecasting three effortless wins. I am forecasting that the most productive offense and stingiest scoring defense will execute enough of the difficult plays to finish the season. Dorrill can review the seven points I have allowed Saffron above the first meeting. I assume he will have notes.

body.text: Ellis Quill — The favorite, and the clubs that learned to continue

Mossdeep is my champion, but Lavender is the team I most want to watch before we get there. The Wails won their last eight games and took Johto East with a 21–20 victory over Blackthorn. They accomplished the last part after losing Mr. Clanky, whose current injury report still lists five weeks. Moth Ball inherited responsibility while the season was being decided. Travis Scarboro’s team kept winning. That is a substantial story even for those of us who would happily write about the Wails all week.

I pick Lavender to beat Vermilion, then upset Saffron. That second choice is my biggest departure from the season’s broad evidence. Saffron scored 597 points and conceded 138; Lavender finished at 325 and 317. Nobody should read those totals and mistake my choice for the safe one. I am giving more weight to the Wails’ recent offensive development and their demonstrated ability to finish uncomfortable games. I expect a close contest, with Lavender finding one more useful possession than the season totals would suggest.

That produces a conference championship at Lavender against Cinnabar. I take the Blaze there. Four successive wins, including victories over Blackthorn and Mt. Silver, give Blaine’s team a real postseason argument. Losing Exploud is a serious subtraction, and the opening rematch with Blackthorn is my hardest first-round choice. Gholdengo must distribute the absent tight end’s work. I think he can, while recognizing that 657 receiving yards are not replaced by an optimistic sentence.

The divisional upset at Mt. Silver follows from that judgment and the Reds’ availability. Cinnabar won the regular-season meeting 38–24. Mt. Silver’s current list includes Tic Thorpe, Josh Alakazam, Tony Gyarzalez and Ariados, as well as new injuries from the finale. The bye offers recovery time, but it does not turn every listed absence into an available player. I cannot select the healthiest version of a familiar team simply because I would like to see it play.

Mossdeep has also had to make choices about who plays and why. Michael Dorrill used the closing weeks to rest starters and give younger players experience, then finished with wins of 22–3 and 27–0. The intent matters. Those scores belong to an organization preparing different players for different responsibilities, rather than a favorite trying to demonstrate its maximum margin every week. The season still ended with 724 points scored and 130 allowed.

I have the Eclipse beating Dewford, Sunyshore and Cinnabar, with a 31–20 Indigo Bowl. Sunyshore is the opponent most likely to interrupt that route: thirteen wins, a defense that conceded 211 points and a coach who will certainly make the occasion feel large enough. My bracket asks Cinnabar to win four games while replacing an important receiver and Mossdeep to win three with a bye first. The latter is the sturdier forecast. I would enjoy being wrong about Lavender’s ceiling and considerably less about the rest of this page.

Cinnabar Blaze at Mt. Silver Reds
Lavender Wails at Saffron Psi Corps

body.text: Dorian Pike — Mt. Silver gets the last argument

Connor McLarren, I am still picking your football team. The 21–13 loss to Cianwood is a thoroughly unpleasant way to enter a bye, and the injury report has become longer than any coach wants to discuss. I have read both. I also remember fourteen wins, 481 points and the 36–33 victory over Saffron. The Reds earned the first seed before the finale. They get a week in which their players do not have to survive another elimination game. I intend to count that advantage.

Garshawn Lynch led the league with 1,200 rushing yards in eleven appearances. That is the starting point of my championship argument. Mt. Silver does not need to ask its available quarterback to imitate every missing passer if Lynch can give the offense productive possessions. The receiving losses make that requirement more urgent, not less possible. I am choosing the Reds’ ability to organize around the player who remains capable of changing a game on the ground.

Cinnabar is the hardest choice on my bracket. I take the Blaze over Blackthorn, then send them to Mt. Silver after wins by Saffron and Lavender. Blaine’s club beat the Reds 38–24 in Week 16 and has won four straight. Anyone who has read me knows I have been rather willing to discuss Cinnabar’s merits. The new six-week entry for Exploud matters. His 657 receiving yards are leaving the offense just as it needs to win away from home. I take Mt. Silver to win the rematch, and I expect that decision to be mentioned to me repeatedly.

Then I take the Reds over Saffron again. Trent Scarboro has the healthier team and the more spectacular point differential. He also had a chance at Mt. Silver in Week 15 and lost 36–33. That does not guarantee the next result. It establishes that this opponent can make his team play a game beyond the comfortable scores that dominate the Psi Corps schedule. Saffron is the club most likely to stop my champion, and I would rather identify the danger plainly than pretend this bracket is a certificate.

My largest upset is Sunyshore winning the Hoenn–Sinnoh championship at Mossdeep. Yes, the Eclipse won the regular-season meeting 27–3. Yes, I have seen 17–0 and the 594-point differential. Karson Jones still has a thirteen-win team, and I expect his defense to force a less comfortable game when everything is at stake. The sixteen-week injury entry for 88 Special is a real obstacle. This pick requires the available receivers to take on more, particularly around Fera LaGatr. That is my judgment, and it is plainly the most exposed part of the bracket.

Rustboro beats Petalburg in my opening round, then loses at Mossdeep. Dewford beats Eterna, then loses at Sunyshore. I finish with Mt. Silver 31, Sunyshore 24 in the Indigo Bowl. The injuries make the Reds a vulnerable champion pick. The bye, the running game and their demonstrated ability to beat Saffron keep them a defensible one. Connor, I have given you the final word on the field. Please make it longer than thirteen points.

body.text: Rowan Vale — Saffron gets one more meeting with Mossdeep

Saffron is my champion. Archam Manning led the league with 4,633 passing yards, HeeDee Lamb caught enough footballs to accumulate 1,878 receiving yards, and NeMarcus Tare collected twenty-nine sacks. Chen Norton Jr added twenty-three. The Psi Corps finished 14–3 with 597 points scored and 138 allowed. I am taking the team that makes opposing protection meetings feel understaffed.

The two three-point defeats at Mossdeep and Mt. Silver are the obvious objections. They are also the reason I can choose Saffron without asking it to discover an entirely new level of football. It lost 20–17 to the undefeated Eclipse and 36–33 to the conference’s first seed. Those games were competitive. The gap between losing them and winning the next one is a football argument I can make. I do not need to invent a weakness in a seventeen-win team to think it can lose once.

My opening upset is Rustboro at Petalburg. The Pride won both regular-season meetings, and I can already hear the reply being typed. Oinkologne remains out with two weeks reported. Rustboro has Philly Gabite’s 870 rushing yards and Gibby Timmy’s 953 receiving yards, and it just put up twenty-nine in a loss. I am choosing the better chance of pushing this particular matchup beyond Petalburg’s preferred total. The Stone defense has to cooperate. Its thirty-five points allowed to Dewford make that a fairly substantial condition.

Cinnabar then beats Mt. Silver in my divisional round. That is the biggest seed upset on my bracket, although Blaine’s club already won their meeting 38–24. The Reds’ bye is useful; their injury list is still severe. I trust Cinnabar’s four-game winning streak and Gholdengo’s distribution enough to survive the new absence of Exploud. Saffron beats Lavender, then beats Cinnabar. The regular-season 35–3 meeting is stronger evidence for that matchup than the argument that the Blaze have become entertaining.

Mossdeep gets Rustboro and Sunyshore on my projected route. I take the Eclipse both times. Its rest-and-development finish makes the last two scoring totals a poor basis for declaring the offense diminished. Michael Dorrill deliberately gave younger players work and still won 22–3 and 27–0. Dram Marino’s fifty-six touchdowns and four interceptions remain available evidence, as do Accel BeckhmJr’s 1,953 receiving yards. The Eclipse are the opponent most likely to make my champion pick look ambitious.

I finish with Saffron 30, Mossdeep 27. My hardest choice is the Bowl itself. Mossdeep has the better record, the larger point differential and the first head-to-head win. Saffron has a healthy current report and a passing-and-pressure combination capable of changing the next meeting. I expect one more successful scoring possession from the Psi Corps than it managed in Week 10. If that fails, Mara will have the numbers ready. She has already had seventeen weeks of practice.

body.text: Tessa Wren — Mossdeep, with Saffron waiting at the end

My bracket ends with Mossdeep 31, Saffron 24. The Eclipse have the strongest completed-season evidence: seventeen wins, 724 points scored and 130 allowed. Their closing development work also succeeded on its own terms. Budew Baker received meaningful starts while the established offense rested, and Mossdeep won both games. That gives Michael Dorrill more usable experience behind his starters, though the playoff depth and actual participants still have to be confirmed when the games arrive.

I take all three higher seeds in Kanto–Johto’s opening round. Saffron has a large production and availability advantage over Olivine. Lavender’s eight straight wins and recent passing improvement give it the edge over Vermilion. Cinnabar–Blackthorn is my hardest wild-card call: the Blaze won the earlier meeting, but Exploud’s new six-week absence removes a productive tight end just before the rematch. Hatterene’s accuracy keeps the Dragons within reach. I give Gholdengo and the home team one more scoring possession.

Those results send Cinnabar to Mt. Silver and Lavender to Saffron. I choose Cinnabar and Saffron. The Blaze’s 38–24 regular-season win at Mt. Silver matters alongside the Reds’ current injuries, rather than as a guarantee of another victory. A bye helps with recovery and removes one game from the route. It cannot justify writing Tic Thorpe or Tony Gyarzalez into a lineup before their availability supports it. Cinnabar over the first seed is my biggest projected upset.

Saffron then beats Cinnabar for the conference title. The 35–3 regular-season result is a useful matchup warning for Blaine, whose offense will already be trying to replace Exploud. Archam Manning has the receiving support to sustain scoring even if one target is contained. Tare and Norton give the defense two established sources of disruption. I expect the Psi Corps to win the extra game required by their second seed and arrive at the Bowl as a serious challenger.

In Hoenn–Sinnoh, I take Sunyshore and Petalburg at home, with Dewford winning at Eterna. I like the Thorns’ defense, which allowed only 184 points, but Stantler, Tatsugiri and Dewgong are all unavailable on the current report. Dewford has the healthier group and just scored thirty-five at Rustboro. Reseeding puts the Breakers at Mossdeep and Petalburg at Sunyshore. I take both higher seeds there, then Mossdeep in the conference championship.

Saffron is the likeliest team to stop the Eclipse. Their 20–17 meeting supplies direct evidence of a close contest, and the Psi Corps currently have no positive-week injury entries. My final choice favors Marino’s efficiency, the range of Mossdeep’s receiving production and a defense that allowed fewer points than any other club. Poury Holt’s six-week absence removes a useful option, but the Eclipse have already demonstrated alternatives. This is a forecast of execution over three games, with the Bowl the hardest of them.

articles.title: Dewford’s return game changes the price of every score
articles.dek: Meowscarada’s finale shows why an opponent cannot finish its preparation at the offensive and defensive playbooks.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Rustboro scored a touchdown and immediately had to defend a ninety-nine-yard kickoff return. That is an expensive way to discover that the scoring drive was only part of the exchange. Dewford’s Meowscarada supplied the return, then later caught the decisive touchdown pass in a 35–29 victory. The Breakers go to Eterna with several ways to change a game that the home team would prefer to keep small.

The return season supports taking that danger seriously. Meowscarada accumulated 978 return yards, two kickoff-return touchdowns and a punt-return touchdown. One spectacular finale does not create those earlier scores. It joins a body of work that earned PSPN’s Hoenn–Sinnoh return-specialist selection. The relevant preparation is specific: coverage discipline, field position and what the defense must do if the offense receives a short field.

Eterna allowed 184 points in seventeen games and won its finale 9–3. That defense has earned respect. Its offense now has reported absences for Tatsugiri, Stantler and Dewgong. A return touchdown would force the available group to produce an answer beyond the modest scoring requirement of the last game. Dewford does not have to repeat a ninety-nine-yard play for the return threat to deserve attention; useful field position can change the length and difficulty of an ordinary scoring drive.

The Breakers also converted eight of eleven third downs at Rustboro. Excadrill rushed for 101 yards and scored. Those details prevent the coverage meeting from becoming the whole opponent report. A defense that overreacts to the explosive possibilities still has to finish the next manageable rushing down, and a team that stops the runner still must contain Frosmoth’s passing opportunities.

Rustboro’s afternoon illustrates the interaction. Shawn Watzon threw for 296 yards without an interception, Gibby Timmy caught 148 and the Stone reached twenty-nine points. Those are useful offensive contributions. Dewford kept finding enough possession value through third downs, a return and timely scoring plays to remain ahead. The final margin was six, so each of those sources mattered to the outcome without requiring a claim that one of them caused everything.

The playoff forecast should account for the opponent’s personnel and preferred game. Eterna has the better season-long points-allowed figure and home field. Dewford arrives with no current positive-week injury entry and a finale in which several units supplied points or sustained possessions. That gives the visitor a credible route to winning even if the Thorns make the passing game less expansive than it was at Rustboro.

I chose Dewford in the opening round. The selection depends on the Breakers making Eterna answer more than one kind of scoring threat. A return touchdown would help enormously, but my pick does not require predicting one. It requires competent coverage of Dewford’s own, productive rushing downs and enough completed drives to make the injured home offense keep responding. The special-teams meeting deserves as much attention as the attractive receiving highlights.

art.alt: Dewford’s return game deserves its own preparation. Conceptual coastal practice-field illustration.

articles.title: Crobat gave Cianwood a final game worth keeping
articles.dek: The Crushers missed the field, but their victory at Mt. Silver remains a complete achievement of its own.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Crobat answered Mt. Silver’s opening touchdown with a ninety-eight-yard kickoff return, then caught both of Cianwood’s second-half touchdowns. The Crushers won 21–13 and finished 8–9. Olivine’s victory kept them outside the playoffs. Both results belong in the account of the afternoon: the invitation did not arrive, and the victory was substantial.

It is easy to let the qualification table reduce the losing side of a race to a short sentence. Cianwood’s players still had to execute a difficult road assignment against the conference’s first seed. The return answered Garshawn Lynch’s early score immediately. The two receiving touchdowns turned a 13–7 halftime deficit into an eight-point lead. A scoreless fourth quarter then required the team to preserve what it had earned.

Crobat finished with four catches for 107 yards and two receiving touchdowns, plus 119 kickoff-return yards and the return score. The long receiving touchdown came on a fifty-yard deep-middle completion; the other covered eleven yards on a short-left pass. Those were different assignments within the same decisive performance. The common result was that Cianwood found the finishing plays Mt. Silver could not match after halftime.

The Reds’ injuries matter when judging the opponent they actually faced. Crem Ftzpatrik threw for 160 yards, and the current availability list is long. That context keeps the upset in proportion. Cianwood still had to stop the available offense, which included Lynch’s eighty-eight rushing yards, and produce twenty-one points of its own. An injured first seed is a specific opponent, not an automatic road victory.

Neither team lost a turnover, and both punted five times. That makes this a useful counterexample to the assumption that an upset must begin with a parade of gifted possessions. Cianwood did not need an interception return or a fumble recovery to explain the result. It needed Crobat’s return, two successful passing finishes and a defense that allowed no second-half points.

The season review and the broader offseason questions can wait until the league’s championship has been decided. This game deserves to remain recognizable before that work begins. It showed a player taking on several important responsibilities and a team completing its final assignment even as another result closed the route beyond it.

Olivine qualified by winning 17–0 at Azalea. Cianwood could not alter that result from Mt. Silver, and its own win did not create a ninth victory retroactively. The final table therefore remains straightforward. So does the final game: the Crushers came back against a fourteen-win club, held their lead through the fourth quarter and left with a road win their supporters can discuss without adding an asterisk to the score.

art.alt: Crobat’s final performance supplied a memorable Cianwood win. Conceptual locker-room still life.

articles.title: Cinnabar has earned attention—and another difficult assignment
articles.dek: The Blaze enter the playoffs with four straight wins and a missing tight end, leaving Blaine another concrete problem to solve.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Cinnabar has won four straight games. Blaine gets to enjoy that sentence for approximately as long as it takes to read the next one: Exploud is out six weeks. The Blaze enter their home playoff opener with a productive passing season, a recent victory over their opponent and a missing receiver who caught fifty-seven passes for 657 yards. Preparation can be encouraging and inconvenient at the same time.

The last win was 13–7 at Pewter. It required a different amount of scoring from the 38–24 victory at Mt. Silver, but it completed the same useful task. Cinnabar finished 12–5 and kept the fourth seed already secured. The team now needs to turn its recent work into a successful rematch with Blackthorn, which arrives after losing its division by one point.

Gholdengo finished with 3,867 passing yards, thirty touchdowns and nine interceptions. That is enough production to support a serious playoff argument. It also helps explain why replacing Exploud involves more than handing an anonymous player a route sheet. The tight end supplied a substantial portion of the completions and yards in that offense. The other targets must make their own work available often enough to sustain the quarterback’s distribution.

Glalie’s twelve-catch, 154-yard, two-touchdown performance against Celadon in the previous round supplies an example of another receiver carrying a large afternoon. It does not announce the Blackthorn target order. Blaine can use it as evidence that the offense has already received meaningful production from another source, then decide how to distribute the next set of responsibilities with the players available.

Arcanine’s remaining one-week absence deserves the same role-aware reading. The season contains eight sacks, even though a simple position label can suggest an offensive player. Cinnabar has to account for the defensive work it is missing as well as the tight-end receptions. Blackthorn’s Hatterene threw for 301 yards in the finale and has thirty-eight passing touchdowns across the season. The rematch is a poor occasion to forget which jobs an injured player was actually doing.

I have Cinnabar advancing from the opening round in my bracket. That choice respects the earlier meeting and the recent sequence of wins. It also accepts a genuine risk: the available offense has changed, while the opponent’s passing production remains substantial. I expect the Blaze to find enough scoring at home, but an early touchdown by Blackthorn would not constitute an inexplicable departure from the evidence.

Cinnabar’s supporters have earned a week of discussing a real championship route. The team has beaten opponents it could meet again, and Gholdengo has completed a productive regular season. The first requirement is narrower and more immediate: replace Exploud’s contribution, protect the quarterback and prevent Hatterene from controlling the passing exchange. Blaine has four consecutive wins behind him and one opponent directly ahead.

articles.title: Injury Report: 88 Special, Exploud and Gabite miss the playoff opening
articles.dek: New losses for Sunyshore, Cinnabar and Olivine; Eterna loses another target, and Mt. Silver’s bye begins with a long availability list.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Sunyshore opens the playoffs without 88 Special, whose new reported absence is sixteen weeks. The receiver finished the regular season with ten receiving touchdowns, including two in the penultimate game. Cinnabar has lost Exploud for six weeks, Olivine has lost Gabite for eight, and Eterna has a new two-week absence for Dewgong. Those changes arrive before home-and-away assignments already fixed by the final standings.
Sunyshore and Cinnabar lose productive targets

88 Special caught two passes for twenty-six yards in the 23–3 win at Veilstone. His season total of 526 receiving yards and ten touchdowns makes the loss substantial before Hearthome visits. Fera LaGatr remains an established option after seventy-three catches for 766 yards, while MF STOMP caught seven passes for seventy-six in the finale. Those are observed contributions; the playoff distribution has not been announced.

Cinnabar’s Exploud finished with fifty-seven catches, 657 yards and four receiving touchdowns. His six-week absence removes a productive tight end before the Blackthorn rematch. Arcanine remains out one reported week; the player’s recorded defensive work includes eight sacks, so treating the listed halfback position as the whole injury impact would miss an important job. Blackthorn also has Exploud out one week and Sawsbuck out four.
Olivine and Eterna face immediate adjustments

Olivine qualified with a shutout at Azalea and now travels to Saffron with Gabite out eight weeks. Gabite accumulated 702 rushing yards. Stantler and Gogoat remain out four weeks apiece, and Beedrill has a new twelve-week absence. The Ironclads must assemble enough offense against a Saffron defense that allowed 138 points; the Psi Corps have no current positive-week injury entry.

Eterna’s new two-week absence for Dewgong removes a receiver with 375 season yards. Tatsugiri remains out six weeks and Stantler one. Slowking completed the finale at quarterback as the Thorns beat Snowpoint 9–3; the prior injury entry alone would not have established that appearance, but the recorded game does. Dewford, Eterna’s wild-card opponent, has no current positive-week injury entry after scoring thirty-five at Rustboro.
The byes offer time, with no guaranteed return

Mt. Silver has new absences for Vibrava, five weeks, and Medicham, four. Tic Thorpe remains out three, Josh Alakazam four, Tony Gyarzalez five, Ariados ten and Ninji Asomugha one. Crem Ftzpatrik threw for 160 yards in the finale and Garshawn Lynch rushed for eighty-eight. The first seed removes one game from the championship route, but it does not make every injured player available for the next one.

Mossdeep’s Poury Holt remains out six weeks. Shawn Mareman rushed for 153 yards and caught a touchdown in the 27–0 finale, useful evidence of another contributor during Michael Dorrill’s confirmed rest-and-development plan. Mareman’s own new entry has zero remaining weeks; it does not establish an additional absence. The bye and the intentional starter rest should be considered alongside the current availability report, without assuming a playoff lineup.
Other wild-card absences

Lavender’s Mr. Clanky remains out five weeks before Vermilion visits. Moth Ball’s 248 passing yards and late division-winning drive provide direct evidence of the available quarterback’s work. Vermilion has Drakloak out nine weeks, Gabite one, Exploud two and Delcatty two. Drakloak’s 755 receiving yards make that continuing absence particularly consequential against the Wails.

Petalburg’s Oinkologne remains out two weeks after a 957-yard rushing season. Rustboro’s Milotic is out four. Hearthome has Dodrio out two and Mr. Mime six before the trip to Sunyshore. All durations below are reported recovery counters, not medical diagnoses or guaranteed return dates. A designation reaching zero does not establish activation, a start or game participation.

articles.title: Wild-card weekend: six games, twelve clubs, no spare week
articles.dek: The complete opening slate and thirty independently authored staff score picks.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Mossdeep and Mt. Silver have the byes. Everyone else must win immediately. Our six full game previews accompany this round overview; the panel below preserves each writer’s own forecast, including the disagreements at Cinnabar and Petalburg. These are editorial predictions, made from the completed regular season and current availability.

matchups.title: Olivine arrives with a berth and an injured backfield
matchups.analysis: The Ironclads earned their invitation with a shutout, then learned that Gabite faces eight weeks out. Saffron has a healthy current report, the league passing-yardage leader and two rushers with at least twenty-three sacks. Drampa must keep this from becoming a succession of obvious passing downs.
matchups.matchup: Olivine arrives with a berth and an injured backfield
matchups.awayKey: Keep Drampa below three sacks and finish two touchdown drives.
matchups.homeKey: Turn the depleted Olivine running game into long third downs.

prediction.reason: Olivine can make Saffron work for an early lead, but the receiving depth around Manning should outlast an offense now missing Gabite and Gogoat. I expect the separation to grow across the game.

matchups.title: Lavender brings its new division title into a different kind of test
matchups.analysis: The Wails won Johto East by one point and have won eight straight. Vermilion finished with three straight wins, none by more than seven. Moth Ball gives Lavender a developing passing story, while Chandelure must create enough scoring without the injured Drakloak.
matchups.matchup: Lavender brings its new division title into a different kind of test
matchups.awayKey: Score at least twenty points without an interception return or short field being required.
matchups.homeKey: Convert the recent passing surge into three touchdown possessions.

prediction.reason: The Wails have won eight straight and just handled the pressure of a division decider. Their passing improvement supplies more repeatable scoring than Vermilion has shown over its three narrow finishing wins.

matchups.title: Cinnabar and Blackthorn meet again with less receiving help
matchups.analysis: The Blaze won at Blackthorn 31–19 in Week 15 and enter on four straight victories. Their finale cost them Exploud for six weeks. Hatterene has 4,532 passing yards for the Dragons, who are also missing Sawsbuck. This rematch asks both quarterbacks to replace important production.
matchups.matchup: Cinnabar and Blackthorn meet again with less receiving help
matchups.awayKey: Protect Hatterene well enough to keep sack losses from ending scoring drives.
matchups.homeKey: Redistribute Exploud’s targets without losing the middle of the passing game.

prediction.reason: Cinnabar’s earlier road win and four-game finish give it a small edge. Hatterene should keep Blackthorn within one possession, while the Blaze need a collective answer to Exploud’s missing targets.

matchups.title: Sunyshore starts a third meeting without 88 Special
matchups.analysis: The Starseekers won the regular-season meetings 28–3 and 53–17. Hearthome has won five straight since the second defeat and carries a different confidence into the rematch. Sunyshore’s finale also brought a sixteen-week injury entry for 88 Special. Karson Jones must adjust a winning offense immediately.
matchups.matchup: Sunyshore starts a third meeting without 88 Special
matchups.awayKey: Hold Sunyshore below twenty-eight points and protect Frosmoth from early giveaways.
matchups.homeKey: Replace 88 Special’s receiving work while sustaining the defensive form of the last two games.

prediction.reason: Sunyshore’s two head-to-head wins and its closing defense outweigh Hearthome’s improved form. The absence of 88 Special should reduce some offensive flexibility, so I am projecting less than the fifty-three from the second meeting.

matchups.title: Rustboro gets a third chance at the division champion
matchups.analysis: Petalburg won both meetings, 30–7 and 17–10, and now hosts a third. Oinkologne remains out with two weeks reported, while Rustboro must recover from conceding thirty-five to Dewford. The Stone have enough rushing and receiving production to make an upset plausible if their defense gives it time.
matchups.matchup: Rustboro gets a third chance at the division champion
matchups.awayKey: Keep Petalburg under twenty points and finish three scoring possessions.
matchups.homeKey: Win first down without Oinkologne and avoid giving Rustboro a possession advantage.

prediction.reason: Petalburg’s two head-to-head wins carry more weight than Rustboro’s extra points in a loss. The absent running back keeps this close, but the Pride have already demonstrated the defensive plan twice.

matchups.title: Dewford’s surge meets Eterna’s reduced offense
matchups.analysis: Eterna allowed only 184 points all season, then won its finale 9–3. Dewford arrives after three straight wins and thirty-five points at Rustboro. The Thorns are missing Stantler, Tatsugiri and now Dewgong, making this a test of whether their defense can leave enough work for the available offense.
matchups.matchup: Dewford’s surge meets Eterna’s reduced offense
matchups.awayKey: Turn two sustained drives into touchdowns rather than settling for field goals.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Dewford below twenty and give Slowking manageable third downs.

prediction.reason: Eterna’s 184 points allowed keep this within reach, but Dewgong’s new injury joins Stantler and Tatsugiri on an already restrictive report. Dewford’s healthier offense gives it a slight road advantage.

articles.title: PSPN’s Pro Bowl: 86 original honorees, and the decisions behind them
articles.dek: Separate conference rosters, starters and reserves, the hardest snubs, and an explicitly unawarded long-snapper slot.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Dram Marino and Archam Manning lead PSPN’s first conference Pro Bowl selections. Accel BeckhmJr and HeeDee Lamb earned starting receiving places, NeMarcus Tare heads a crowded Kanto–Johto outside-linebacker group, and players from eliminated clubs receive the same consideration as the fourteen postseason entrants. These are PSPN’s editorial honors for the completed regular season.

Each conference has forty-three selections. The long-snapper slot is explicitly unawarded because no identifiable snapping assignment or individual snapping record is available. We retain the other positional allocations, including a separate punter, return specialist and coverage specialist. The three-player safety group has two starters; we do not invent free-safety and strong-safety distinctions.

Starters and reserves were selected together and are all original honorees. Injuries and eventual Indigo Bowl participation do not remove eligibility. No game has been scheduled by this article, and these choices do not represent the game’s official awards or a fabricated fan, player or coach vote. There is no guaranteed team representative or team cap.

Positions follow observed football jobs, supported by lineup history and production. Players who changed jobs are evaluated for the role being honored; an earlier position label does not automatically decide the ballot. Offensive-line selections use verified tackle, guard and center assignments, workload and the performance of the units they supported. Complete individual season blocking grades are unavailable, so those honors carry more uncertainty than the passing or receiving selections. Team output is context, not a claim that one blocker caused every yard.

body.text: Manning and Marino start; the reserve decisions differ

Manning receives the Kanto–Johto start for 4,633 passing yards and forty-three touchdowns across seventeen games. Blackthorn’s Hatterene completed 377 of 517 passes for 4,532 yards, thirty-eight touchdowns and eight interceptions, a compelling accuracy and ball-security case. Manning’s greater scoring production and nineteen sacks taken, compared with fifty for Hatterene, tip the start. Protection is shared work, so the sack difference is supporting context rather than an individual fault total.

Gholdengo takes the third Kanto–Johto place with 3,867 yards, thirty touchdowns and nine interceptions. Vermilion’s Chandelure, with 3,104 yards, twenty-one touchdowns and eleven interceptions, is the closest conventional alternative considered here. Gholdengo supplies more passing production and fewer interceptions over the same seventeen-game span. The playoff berth alone does not settle either case.

Marino’s 4,341 yards, fifty-six touchdowns and four interceptions make him the Hoenn–Sinnoh starter. His fifteen appearances reflect Mossdeep’s confirmed late rest policy. DeZhaun Watzon earns a reserve place with twenty-nine touchdowns and nine interceptions in fourteen appearances. Sootopolis’s Drampa takes the other with 3,169 yards and twenty-five touchdowns. Snowpoint’s Drampa has fewer interceptions, seven against twelve, but trails the Sootopolis quarterback by 243 yards and five touchdowns. We favor the larger scoring contribution for the last place.
Lynch’s start and Skattebo’s new job

Garshawn Lynch rushed for 1,200 yards on 155 carries in eleven appearances, then added 292 receiving yards and four receiving touchdowns to eleven rushing scores. That efficiency earns the start over Dam Skattebo, whose 1,026 rushing yards and eighteen rushing touchdowns make him an emphatic reserve. Skattebo’s earlier defensive-end assignments do not describe the offensive job that produced his selection: his sustained later running-back work and 183 carries establish that role.

Viridian’s Gabite receives the third place with 1,126 rushing yards and 319 carries. Cianwood’s Bibarel is the major omission: 1,087 yards, four rushing touchdowns and a lower carry total of 284. Gabite has thirty-nine more rushing yards and ninety-six receiving yards to Bibarel’s thirty-one. The modest advantage in total backfield production decides a close final place; neither runner approaches the efficiency of the starter.

Ninjaskamara starts for Hoenn–Sinnoh after 1,138 rushing yards, twenty rushing touchdowns and another 306 receiving yards in twelve appearances. Philly Gabite’s eleven rushing touchdowns and Petalburg Oinkologne’s 957 rushing yards earn the reserves. Snowpoint’s Oinkologne amassed 943 rushing yards and 218 receiving yards, but no rushing or receiving touchdowns and six lost fumbles. Petalburg’s runner supplied six combined offensive touchdowns without a recorded lost fumble, which decides that comparison.

Mothel Irving and Mauville’s Mothim are the fullbacks. Both have sustained observed fullback assignments despite receiving-centered production. Irving’s sixty-eight catches, 893 yards and six touchdowns beat Cinnabar Greninja’s seventy-two catches, 692 yards and five scores. Mothim’s seventy-nine catches and 733 yards lead his conference’s comparable fullback work. Neither selection implies an unavailable individual blocking grade.
The fourth receiver places are expensive

Lamb and Gengar Pickens start for Kanto–Johto. Lamb’s ninety-five catches, 1,878 yards and eighteen receiving touchdowns set him apart; Pickens adds 936 yards and eight scores in fifteen appearances. Mahogany’s Dugtrio and Mt. Silver’s Gregar Jenings take the reserves. Dugtrio has 800 receiving yards and seven touchdowns; Jenings has 795 and six. Blackthorn’s Ninjask, with 705 yards and eight touchdowns, is the toughest scoring-based snub. We favor Jenings’ additional ninety yards and forty catches over thirty-seven, while recognizing the two-touchdown advantage Ninjask surrendered in this decision.

Accel BeckhmJr’s 1,953 yards and thirty-two touchdowns lead Hoenn–Sinnoh. Gibby Timmy starts beside him after 953 yards on forty-one catches. Ninjulio Jones takes one reserve place with 770 yards and seven scores; Veilstone’s rookie Ponyta gets the other with 750 yards and five. Snowpoint’s Drakloak matched Ponyta’s forty-eight catches and five scores but finished eighteen yards behind, with three lost fumbles against none. That narrow receiving comparison decides the fourth place.

Sunyshore’s 88 Special scored ten receiving touchdowns, a strong argument against that decision. His 526 yards and thirty-seven catches nevertheless trail Ponyta’s broader receiving workload by 224 yards and eleven catches. We choose the larger body of receiving work for this roster. The new injury does not disqualify 88 Special; the same comparison would apply if he were healthy.

Tony Gyarzalez starts at Kanto–Johto tight end with seventy-five catches, 948 yards and seven touchdowns despite his current absence. Fuchsia’s Heatmor gets the reserve place with seventy catches and 850 yards. Cinnabar’s Exploud has one more receiving touchdown than Heatmor, but 193 fewer yards and thirteen fewer catches. Gronkaludon starts in Hoenn–Sinnoh, ahead of Fera LaGatr, on 830 yards and nine touchdowns against 766 and five. Both are full honorees.
The line selections reward sustained responsibility

Saffron’s Crustle, Drampa and Rhyhorn occupy starting tackle, guard and center places alongside Mt. Silver’s Steel Hutchins and Larry Aggron. Each logged at least 907 offensive snaps. Their units supported 597 and 481 team points, respectively, and the two offenses produced the conference’s leading passing and rushing seasons. Lavender’s Vikavolt and Walrein provide tackle and guard reserves; Gole Upshaw is the reserve center. Their selections recognize sustained work within productive units without inventing clean-sheet pass-protection totals.

Mossdeep’s Crust Alstott, Tyran Armstead and Bastony Boseli start at tackle, guard and center for Hoenn–Sinnoh. Sunyshore’s Garg Williams and Lair Thuney complete the starting five. Rustboro’s Aggron and Pupitar are the tackle and guard reserves, while Hearthome’s Musharna is the reserve center. Armstead’s 652 offensive snaps are fewer than several alternatives, but his established guard work supported the league’s highest-scoring offense before the deliberate late-season rest. The other selected linemen supplied 855 or more offensive snaps.

Fuchsia’s Skeledirge and Bronzong each played 922 offensive snaps and have credible workload arguments at tackle. We favor Lavender’s Vikavolt for the reserve place based on the full-season responsibility in a division-winning offense, while acknowledging that team success cannot isolate blocking quality. At Hoenn–Sinnoh guard, Petalburg’s Araquanid supplied 865 snaps; Pupitar’s 908 and Rustboro’s greater scoring production tip our final choice. These are the most judgment-dependent positions on the ballot.
Outside linebacker produces the hardest defensive cuts

Tare and Chen Norton Jr start in Kanto–Johto. Tare recorded twenty-nine sacks and sixty-five pressures; Norton had twenty-three sacks, sixty-six pressures and eleven tackles for loss. Blayz Matthews takes the third place with 17.5 sacks, seventy pressures and sixteen tackles for loss. Tare’s documented move from cornerback to outside linebacker is reflected here. His pass-rush production and established later assignment support the honor at that job, rather than a convenient extra place in the secondary.

Verrick Brooks has a powerful snub case: seventy-five pressures, thirteen sacks and ten tackles for loss in eleven appearances. Matthews supplies 4.5 more sacks, six more tackles for loss and six more appearances, enough to outweigh Brooks’ five-pressure advantage. Mahogany’s Bruxish produced fifteen sacks over seventeen games, and Vermilion’s Volbeat had fourteen. Neither displaces a selected trio with greater finishing production and substantial broader disruption.

Derrat Brooks starts for Hoenn–Sinnoh with 15.5 sacks, three interceptions and twelve passes defended. Mauville rookie Volbeat gets the other start with thirteen sacks and forty-three tackles. Joey Sporeter takes the reserve place with 12.5 sacks and forty-one pressures. Sunyshore’s Fred Whirler is the difficult omission: 9.5 sacks, forty-one pressures, ten tackles for loss and fifty-five tackles. Sporeter’s three additional sacks decide the last place, while Volbeat’s larger tackle contribution and slightly higher sack total decide the second starting designation.

Olivine’s Darmanitan and Pewter’s Iron Leaves start at defensive end, with Cianwood’s Leafeon in reserve. We preserve the end/linebacker distinction rather than moving an outside linebacker into this group. Darmanitan’s twelve sacks and fifty-one pressures lead the selected ends. Iron Leaves has nine sacks, forty-six pressures and an interception; Leafeon has 9.5 sacks and forty-five pressures. The interception gives Iron Leaves the narrow starting edge, while both receive the honor.

Oreburgh’s Drednaw and Canalave’s Passimian start at Hoenn–Sinnoh end; Lavaridge’s Passimian is the reserve. Their sack totals are 11.5, ten and nine. Mauville’s Drednaw has forty-eight pressures, one more than Canalave’s Passimian and six more than Lavaridge’s, but six sacks. The selected players’ stronger finishing production decides those places, with pressure retained as an important counterargument.
Interior disruption and coverage beyond the playoff field

Mauler Twin and Celadon’s Klawf #22 start inside for Kanto–Johto, with Cinnabar’s Beartic in reserve. Mauler Twin combines 4.5 sacks with forty-seven pressures and nine tackles for loss; Klawf has seven sacks and seven tackles for loss. Beartic’s eleven tackles for loss and four sacks edge Olivine Mamoswine’s eleven tackles for loss and two sacks, despite Mamoswine’s larger pressure total. Blackthorn’s Whiscash and Olivine’s Octillery are the inside linebackers: ninety-two and 104 tackles, with fifteen and sixteen tackles for loss.

Lavaridge’s Ursaluna and Eterna’s Klawf start on the Hoenn–Sinnoh interior. Ursaluna recorded 7.5 sacks and sixteen tackles for loss; Klawf had six sacks and thirty-five pressures. Rustboro’s Smoke Break gets the reserve place for fourteen tackles for loss, ahead of Torten Carter’s eight, accepting Carter’s pressure advantage of twenty-eight to fourteen. Canalave’s Weezing starts at inside linebacker with 106 tackles and thirteen tackles for loss. Don Philliams takes the reserve place for sixteen tackles for loss and 5.5 sacks, ahead of Veilstone Muk’s larger tackle total but lower backfield production.

Viridian’s Sigilyph and Mahogany’s Lopunny start at cornerback with eleven and seven interceptions, plus twenty-eight and twenty-six passes defended. Lavender’s Picasso adds six interceptions and twenty-two passes defended in reserve. Violet’s Milotic gets the last place with five and sixteen. Azalea’s Gliscor has twenty-five passes defended but three interceptions; we favor Milotic’s two additional takeaways. Tauros Woodson’s four interceptions and eighteen passes defended also leave him just outside.

Venusaur and Dewford’s Gliscor start in Hoenn–Sinnoh with eight and six interceptions. Sootopolis’s Kingdra, six interceptions and eighteen passes defended in thirteen games, gets a reserve place. Rustboro’s Joe takes the fourth on thirty-two passes defended and three interceptions. Petalburg rookie Toedscruel has five interceptions and fifteen passes defended; Mossdeep’s Darrell Revis has five and thirteen. Joe’s much larger defended-pass total earns our final place. Fortree’s Kingdra, with thirty passes defended and three interceptions, is another close omission.

Cinnabar rookie Tatsugiri and Mahogany’s Frosmoth start at safety, each with five interceptions. Pach Tatum gets the Kanto–Johto reserve place: eighteen passes defended and seven tackles for loss outweigh Blackthorn Politoed’s extra two interceptions. Electric Berry starts in Hoenn–Sinnoh with five interceptions and nineteen passes defended, beside Sootopolis’s Pachirisu, whose ninety tackles and twelve passes defended accompany three interceptions. Ronnie Watt takes the reserve place with seventy-five tackles, fourteen passes defended and two interceptions. Mauville’s Togekiss has five interceptions but a smaller defensive workload and four passes defended; the sustained safety responsibility decides that last comparison.
Specialists earn separate honors

Blackthorn’s Cacturne is the Kanto–Johto kicker after making twenty of twenty-three field goals, with a long of fifty-eight. Lavender’s Just a cactus made eighteen of twenty-one and all thirty-five extra points, an excellent case sharpened by the division-winning finale. Cacturne’s two additional field goals and longer successful kick take the place. Mahogany’s Watchog is the punter: fourteen inside-the-twenty punts from thirty-eight attempts, with a 49.6-yard gross average. Cacturne averaged 51.7 with fourteen inside twenty from forty-seven. Watchog’s stronger inside-twenty rate decides the punting honor; the roles are assessed separately.

Veilstone’s Sunflora takes the Hoenn–Sinnoh kicking place with thirteen of fourteen field goals and twenty of twenty-one extra points. Eterna’s Vikavolt made twenty-one field goals, but missed five of twenty-six and three of twenty extra points. We favor Sunflora’s accuracy while recognizing the lower field-goal volume. Adam Vinathorn is the punter, with eleven inside twenty from twenty-six punts and a 50.6-yard gross average. Eterna’s Vikavolt supplied far more punts, seventy-eight, but a lower inside-twenty proportion at twenty of seventy-eight. Vinathorn’s placement earns the place despite the smaller workload.

Jolt Train Ln leads Kanto–Johto returners with 1,386 return yards and five punt-return touchdowns. Dewford’s Meowscarada takes Hoenn–Sinnoh with 978 return yards, two kickoff-return touchdowns and one punt-return touchdown. Eterna’s Froslass has more return yards, 1,112, but no return touchdown; Mauville’s Dragapult has 1,077 and two punt-return scores. Meowscarada’s three scores and 23.3 yards per combined return decide a close multi-format comparison.

Vermilion’s Galvantula and Pastoria’s Kilowattrel are the coverage specialists, with forty-one and thirty-one special-teams tackles. Mahogany’s Sandy Shocks has thirty-five and Dewford’s Infernape twenty-six, the strongest omitted tackle totals in their respective conferences. These honors use recorded coverage work rather than treating a spare offensive or defensive roster place as a special-teams selection. Long snapper remains unawarded in both conferences.
